slides.title: What Is Bias, Really?
slides.content: Biases are mental shortcuts your brain uses to make decisions quickly. Everyone has them — they are NOT a sign of stupidity! Your brain evolved these shortcuts over hundreds of thousands of years to keep you alive.
slides.tip: 💡 Key insight: The first step to beating bias is admitting you have it.

slides.title: Your Brain Team: Two Systems
slides.content:
Your brain has two parts working together:

🦸 Amygdala (The Jumpy Superhero) — Reacts in just 20 milliseconds! It's emotional and fast, but sometimes wrong.

🧑‍🔬 Prefrontal Cortex (The Smart One) — Takes 100+ ms to decide. It's rational and careful, but slower.

The catch? For teens, the prefrontal cortex is still developing until about age 25!
slides.tip: 💡 The emotional brain is 20x FASTER — that's why you react before you think!

slides.title: Why Your Brain Is Built This Way
slides.content:
In prehistoric times, your ancestors faced tigers and needed tribes to survive. Running from a rock (safe mistake) was better than getting eaten (deadly mistake). Being rejected by the tribe meant death.

Today, your ancient survival software is running in a modern world of smartphones and social media. The threats have changed, but your brain's shortcuts haven't!
slides.tip: 💡 Biases aren't bugs — they're survival features that sometimes misfire today.

slides.title: Confirmation Bias: The 'I Knew It!' Trap
slides.content:
You seek information that supports what you already believe. When you find it, your brain releases dopamine (the reward chemical) — making you feel good!

This creates a dangerous loop: believe → seek proof → feel rewarded → believe harder.

To fight it: Actively seek opinions that disagree with yours. Ask 'What would prove me wrong?'
slides.tip: 💡 If nothing could change your mind, you're defending a position, not seeking truth.

slides.title: Anchoring Bias: Why the First Number Sticks
slides.content:
Your brain over-relies on the first piece of information (the 'anchor') and doesn't adjust enough.

Example: A shirt priced at $60 seems like a great deal when the original price was $120 — even if $60 is still overpriced!

To fight it: Ask 'Would I pay this if I saw it for the first time?' Research the actual market price.
slides.tip: 💡 The first number is rarely the correct number. Always question the anchor.

slides.title: Bandwagon Effect: Jumping on Board
slides.content:
You tend to believe or do something just because many others are, regardless of evidence. Your brain is wired to follow the group for safety.

Examples: Viral challenges, fads, holding back your opinion because 'nobody else thinks that.'

To fight it: Ask 'Would I believe this if no one else did? Where is the evidence?'
slides.tip: 💡 Popularity is not proof. Facts don't need a crowd to be true.

slides.title: More Brain Shortcuts to Watch For
slides.content:
Halo Effect: One good trait makes you assume they have other good traits. (Good at sports → must be smart/kind)

Blind-Spot Bias: You see bias in others easily, but not in yourself.

Availability Bias: You judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. (Plane crashes seem common because they're in the news, but driving is much more dangerous.)
slides.tip: 💡 Smartest people are those who know they might be wrong.

slides.title: The SMART Check for Sources
slides.content:
Before believing any information, check:

S — Source: Who wrote this? What's their agenda?
M — Motive: Why was this created?
A — Accuracy: Can you verify with another source?
R — Recency: Is this information up to date?
T — Two sides: What's missing from this story?
slides.tip: 💡 Accurate information is usually boring, not exciting. If a headline makes you furious or ecstatic, that's a red flag!

questions.q: What is the Amygdala's reaction time compared to the Prefrontal Cortex?
options: They react at the same speed
Amygdala is 20ms, Prefrontal Cortex is 100+ ms
questions.explanation: The Amygdala (emotional brain) reacts in just 20ms, while the Prefrontal Cortex (rational brain) takes 100+ ms. This speed difference is why you sometimes react emotionally before thinking rationally!

questions.q: Until what age does the Prefrontal Cortex typically keep developing?
questions.explanation: The Prefrontal Cortex (the 'Smart One' that handles rational thinking) keeps developing until about age 25. This is why teenagers often rely more on emotional reactions!

questions.q: What chemical does your brain release when you find information that confirms your beliefs?
questions.explanation: Dopamine — the reward chemical! This is why Confirmation Bias feels so good. Your brain literally rewards you for finding supporting evidence, creating a dangerous feedback loop.

questions.q: In Anchoring Bias, what does the 'anchor' refer to?
options: A heavy weight holding you back
The first piece of information you receive
questions.explanation: The 'anchor' is the first piece of information you receive. Your brain uses it as a reference point and doesn't adjust enough from it — like a $120 original price making $60 seem like a great deal.

questions.q: What should you ask yourself to fight the Bandwagon Effect?
options: Would I believe this if no one else did?
Is this trending on social media?
How many likes does this have?
questions.explanation: 'Would I believe this if no one else did?' This question removes the social pressure and forces you to evaluate the actual evidence. Popularity is not proof!

questions.q: The Halo Effect makes you assume someone has other good traits because they have:
questions.explanation: One good trait! If someone is good at sports, the Halo Effect makes you assume they're also smart and kind — even without evidence. One positive trait 'spills over' to create a glowing overall impression.

options: Not being able to see physically
Seeing bias in others but not yourself
questions.explanation: Seeing bias in others but not yourself! It's the easiest bias to spot in other people and the hardest to see in yourself. That's why self-reflection is so important.

questions.q: According to Error Management Theory, why did biases evolve?
questions.explanation: To help us survive! Biases evolved over hundreds of thousands of years. Better a safe mistake (running from a rock) than a deadly one (getting eaten). Your brain prioritized survival over accuracy.

questions.q: What is a red flag that a headline might be biased or manipulative?
options: It makes you furious or ecstatic
questions.explanation: If a headline makes you furious or ecstatic, that's a red flag! Accurate information is usually boring, not exciting. Strong emotional reactions are designed to bypass your rational thinking.

questions.q: What does the 'T' in SMART Check stand for?
questions.explanation: Two sides — what's missing from this story? The SMART Check stands for Source, Motive, Accuracy, Recency, and Two sides. Always ask what information is being left out!

scenarios.title: 🛒 Shopping Scenario
scenarios.text: You see a pair of headphones 'originally $200, now $80!' The brand is unknown, but the discount seems huge. Your friend says they're amazing.

choices.text: Buy them immediately — 60% off is a steal!
choices.feedback: ❌ Anchoring Bias! The '$200' price is the anchor. You don't know if $80 is actually fair for these headphones. Always research the real market price first.

choices.text: Check reviews and compare prices with other brands first
choices.feedback: ✅ Great thinking! You questioned the anchor and sought independent evidence. This is how you beat Anchoring Bias.

choices.text: Buy them because your friend recommended them
choices.feedback: ⚠️ Bandwagon Effect + Halo Effect! Your friend's opinion is valuable, but it shouldn't replace your own research. They might have different needs or be biased too.

scenarios.title: 📱 Social Media Scenario
scenarios.text: A viral post claims a celebrity did something terrible. Thousands have shared it. The source is a gossip blog you've never heard of.

choices.text: Share it to warn your friends
choices.feedback: ❌ Bandwagon + Availability Bias! Just because many people share it doesn't make it true. Viral misinformation spreads exactly this way.

choices.text: Check reputable news sources before believing or sharing
choices.feedback: ✅ Excellent! You used the SMART Check. Reputable sources, verification, and waiting for facts are how you fight bias in the information age.

choices.text: Believe it because 'where there's smoke, there's fire'
choices.feedback: ⚠️ Confirmation Bias! You're assuming guilt without evidence. 'Smoke' can be manufactured. Always demand evidence, not assumptions.

scenarios.title: 👥 Group Project Scenario
scenarios.text: In a group project, someone disagrees with your idea. You feel defensive and want to prove them wrong.

choices.text: Defend your idea strongly and list why they're wrong
choices.feedback: ⚠️ Confirmation Bias + Ego Protection! Your brain is trying to protect your self-image. But genuine growth comes from considering other perspectives.

choices.text: Genuinely consider their point and look for merit in it
choices.feedback: ✅ Perfect! You activated your Prefrontal Cortex instead of letting your Amygdala react. This is how smart people make better decisions.

choices.text: Agree with them to avoid conflict
choices.feedback: ⚠️ Bandwagon Effect! Just going along isn't the same as genuine consideration. You're still not using critical thinking — you're just avoiding it.

scenarios.title: 🏫 School Election Scenario
scenarios.text: Your school is voting for class president. The most popular student is running, and everyone says they'll vote for them.

choices.text: Vote for them too — they're obviously the best choice
choices.feedback: ❌ Bandwagon Effect! Popularity doesn't equal capability. You're following the crowd instead of evaluating the candidates yourself.

choices.text: Research each candidate's actual plans and qualifications
choices.feedback: ✅ Outstanding! You removed social pressure and evaluated based on evidence. This is independent thinking at its best.

choices.text: Vote for the underdog because going against the crowd is cool
choices.feedback: ⚠️ Reverse Bandwagon! You're still letting the crowd dictate your choice — just in the opposite direction. Evaluate candidates on merit, not popularity or rebellion.

scenarios.title: 📰 News Headline Scenario
scenarios.text: You read a headline: 'SHOCKING: Popular Drink Causes Cancer!' It makes you feel scared and angry.

choices.text: Stop drinking it immediately and tell everyone
choices.feedback: ❌ Multiple biases! The headline used emotional manipulation (fear/anger) to bypass your thinking. You reacted with your Amygdala, not your Prefrontal Cortex.

choices.text: Check the actual study, sample size, and who funded the research
choices.feedback: ✅ Brilliant detective work! You recognized the emotional manipulation and sought the actual evidence. This is exactly how to evaluate sensational claims.

choices.text: Ignore it because everything causes cancer these days
choices.feedback: ⚠️ Availability Bias in reverse! Just because you've seen many such claims doesn't mean this one is false. Each claim deserves independent evaluation.

scenarios.title: 🎵 Music Opinion Scenario
scenarios.text: You strongly dislike a popular musician. A friend asks you to name something impressive about them.

choices.feedback: ❌ Confirmation Bias! You're so committed to your negative view that you can't find ANY merit. If nothing could change your mind, you're defending a position, not seeking truth.

choices.text: Try to find at least one thing you can acknowledge
choices.feedback: ✅ Excellent! This exercise forces your brain to consider disconfirming evidence. It's uncomfortable but it's how you grow and overcome bias.

choices.text: Change the subject to avoid answering
choices.feedback: ⚠️ Avoidance! You're protecting your existing belief by refusing to engage. Growth requires discomfort sometimes.

cases.title: Case #1: The Influencer Post
cases.text: An influencer posts: 'This skincare product completely changed my life! I've never looked better. Use my code SKIN20 for 20% off! #ad #skincare #glowup'

clues.text: They use their own discount code
'Completely changed my life' is extreme language
Only positive claims, no downsides mentioned
#ad tag is present but might be overlooked
clues.bias: Sponsored content disguised as genuine opinion

cases.title: Case #2: The News Article
cases.text: Headline: 'LOCAL TEEN SAVES DOZENS IN HEROIC ACT!' Article: A teenager helped an elderly neighbor carry groceries. Only 3 sentences long.

clues.text: 'Dozens' is a huge exaggeration for helping one person
Very short article with dramatic headline
Uses emotional words like 'heroic' to grab attention
No sources or verification of the event

cases.title: Case #3: The Online Review
cases.text: Product review: '1 STAR! TERRIBLE! Broke after 2 days! DO NOT BUY! Worst company ever! Save your money!' Posted same day as 50 other 1-star reviews.

clues.text: Extreme language with ALL CAPS shouting
Posted on same day as many similar reviews
No details about how it broke or usage
Only negative, no attempt at balanced view

cases.title: Case #4: The Political Meme
cases.text: Meme shows a politician with a quote: 'I hate poor people and want them to suffer.' No source cited. Shared 50,000 times.

clues.text: Quote seems too extreme to be real
Designed to provoke strong negative emotion
High share count used as credibility signal
